# Objective - Closes #786 - Closes #2252 - Closes #2588 This PR implements a derive macro that allows users to define their queries as structs with named fields. ## Example ```rust #[derive(WorldQuery)] #[world_query(derive(Debug))] struct NumQuery<'w, T: Component, P: Component> { entity: Entity, u: UNumQuery<'w>, generic: GenericQuery<'w, T, P>, } #[derive(WorldQuery)] #[world_query(derive(Debug))] struct UNumQuery<'w> { u_16: &'w u16, u_32_opt: Option<&'w u32>, } #[derive(WorldQuery)] #[world_query(derive(Debug))] struct GenericQuery<'w, T: Component, P: Component> { generic: (&'w T, &'w P), } #[derive(WorldQuery)] #[world_query(filter)] struct NumQueryFilter { _u_16: With, _u_32: With, _or: Or<(With, Changed, Added)>, _generic_tuple: (With, With

), _without: Without>, _tp: PhantomData<(T, P)>, } fn print_nums_readonly(query: Query, NumQueryFilter>) { for num in query.iter() { println!("{:#?}", num); } } #[derive(WorldQuery)] #[world_query(mutable, derive(Debug))] struct MutNumQuery<'w, T: Component, P: Component> { i_16: &'w mut i16, i_32_opt: Option<&'w mut i32>, } fn print_nums(mut query: Query>) { for num in query.iter_mut() { println!("{:#?}", num); } } ``` ## TODOs: - [x] Add support for `&T` and `&mut T` - [x] Test - [x] Add support for optional types - [x] Test - [x] Add support for `Entity` - [x] Test - [x] Add support for nested `WorldQuery` - [x] Test - [x] Add support for tuples - [x] Test - [x] Add support for generics - [x] Test - [x] Add support for query filters - [x] Test - [x] Add support for `PhantomData` - [x] Test - [x] Refactor `read_world_query_field_type_info` - [x] Properly document `readonly` attribute for nested queries and the static assertions that guarantee safety - [x] Test that we never implement `ReadOnlyFetch` for types that need mutable access - [x] Test that we insert static assertions for nested `WorldQuery` that a user marked as readonly
pr_comments: @MinerSebas makes good arguments; I think I'm in favor of this position.

There was a suggestion from Mathspy (in Discord) to wrap all macro attributes to look like this: `#[bevy(read_only)]`. I like it, but I am also inclined to procrastinate this change, as none of our macros does the same, so I guess it can be a part of a separate effort to clean up our macro code.

Upd (16-Jan): I actually ended up wrapping the attributes into `fetch` or `filter_fetch`.
Could the `#[read_only]` attribute be reversed, and everything being read only by default, unless there is a `#[mutable]` attribute?

@mockersf done in the new commit, it seems to look better indeed. Btw, I've just realized my example in the PR description was outdated: the attribute now applies to structs instead of individual fields.

The CI fail seems to be unrelated.

First: this is great work! I don't have any comments on the current impl. This is a really complicated derive, but it serves to hide complexity (and unsafety) from users, which justifies the complexity from my perspective.

I couldn't find a better solution to the "lifetime on state struct" hack currently in use. It is "safe", given that the lifetime isn't actually used anywhere.   

However `FetchedItem` feels "wrong" to me. It took me awhile to figure out why, but I finally sorted it out: it walks back "up" the trait dependency tree, at the cost of redundancy (the correlation is already specified in the other direction), potential for error (you can set FetchedItem::Query to literally anything ... bevy still compiles if I change `&T`'s `FetchedItem::Query` to `With<T>`), type complexity (even more traits and impls in one of the most complicated areas of Bevy), and a loss of "many to one" behavior (bevy_ecs supports more than one WorldQuery type returning the same fetched type ... FetchedItem can only be implemented for one type. this is why the "bool unit type FetchedItem hack" in this PR is required).

This feels resolvable. Note that as written, this isn't _just_ a Fetch derive. Its also a `WorldQuery` derive, with the constraint that the Fetched fields match the WorldQueried fields. Up until now, WorldQuery was the "top" of the hierarchy. We just need to restore that:

* Only accept WorldQuery fields in WorldQuery derives (not FetchedItem fields). Ex: Specify `&'w mut Foo` instead of `Mut<'w, Foo>`. 
* Auto-generate the Fetch, State, and Fetch::Item types by walking down the associated WorldQuery associated types
* Change the derive name from Fetch to WorldQuery to illustrate that it is a WorldQuery derive / "the top of the hierarchy".

This has the added benefit of supporting the types our users are already used to specifying (ex: users use `&mut T` in queries). Most users don't worry about `Mut<T>`. This would also mean that it would transparently update returned values if we ever add the ability to disable change detection for components (ex: no need to change `Mut<T>` back to `&mut T` in these derives when change detection is disabled for `T`).

The one downside is that it means that users are no longer directly defining the types they are retrieving. I personally think this is "acceptable", given the added complexity and tradeoffs of the current impl.

> Only accept WorldQuery fields in WorldQuery derives (not FetchedItem fields). Ex: Specify &'w mut Foo instead of Mut<'w, Foo>

This is a nice ergonomics win.

> Auto-generate the Fetch, State, and Fetch::Item types by walking down the associated WorldQuery associated types

Makes sense.

> Change the derive name from Fetch to WorldQuery to illustrate that it is a WorldQuery derive / "the top of the hierarchy".

This is much clearer: users should be reasoning about `WorldQuery`, not the internals of `Fetch` and `FilterFetch`.

> The one downside is that it means that users are no longer directly defining the types they are retrieving. I personally think this is "acceptable", given the added complexity and tradeoffs of the current impl.

Agreed. This is niche functionality, and we already have this indirection in normal queries (e.g. you ask for `&mut T` but get back a `Mut<T>`).

> > Change the derive name from Fetch to WorldQuery to illustrate that it is a WorldQuery derive / "the top of the hierarchy".
> 
> I also wanted to name it as `WorldQuery`, but I changed it to `Fetch` as I needed to pick a name for the filter derive... And we don't have anything like `WorldQueryFilter`. So I thought `Fetch` and `FetchFilter` would be the closest. I guess we can introduce a `#[world_query(filter)]` attribute to be able to distinguish queries from filters, but I didn't go that way initially to avoid making the code even more complex.

I had the same "Problem" in bevy_lint and choose to call it [FilterQuery](https://github.com/MinerSebas/bevy_lint/blob/main/src/system_lints/model.rs#L89).

> Are you suggesting to return &mut T to users as well? I'm afraid this will remove the ability to access DetectChanges API and perform a read (via as_ref) without triggering a change detection.

Nope! I'm suggesting users defining what amounts to a "group of WorldQueries" (via a WorldQuery derive) and then having the derive auto-generate the "returned struct" based on the contents of the "source query struct". What you outlined in your `MyStruct` example is exactly what I was suggesting.


> If a user decides to pass a returned value from the iterator to some function, they'll likely declare it to accept the original struct (MyStruct in the example - the one to which we applied the derive), but passing the iterator items to it won't compile. Figuring out that you have to use MyStructQuery instead of MyStruct will be quite unintuitive.

Yup this is the biggest downside from my perspective. Thats what I was calling out when I said this: "The one downside is that it means that users are no longer directly defining the types they are retrieving. I personally think this is "acceptable", given the added complexity and tradeoffs of the current impl."

> This will be extremely IDE unfriendly.

It is worth calling out that the current derive is equally IDE unfriendly. Both implementations rely on the same principles to work properly. If the IDE doesn't support proc_macros + trait hierarchies, neither approach will resolve. Fortunately, rust-analyzer already handle these cases fine (otherwise, the "normal" bevy queries wouldn't resolve properly).

> I also wanted to name it as WorldQuery, but I changed it to Fetch as I needed to pick a name for the filter derive... And we don't have anything like WorldQueryFilter

Given that filters are just WorldQueries with `Fetch: FilterFetch`, and FilterFetch is implemented for any Fetch that returns a bool, I think expanding the `WorldQuery` derive with `#[world_query(filter)]` makes the most sense to me. This also moves "fetch" as a concept back into "bevy_ecs internals", which is probably where it belongs. Fetch largely exists because GATs aren't a thing yet for lifetimes. As soon as they are, we can consider removing Fetch entirely.

> I haven't been able to confirm that. I'm a CLion user, maybe there's some sort of experimental flag for rust-analyzer that I'm not aware of? Neither CLion nor rust-analyzer resolve regular queries for me. Afaik, CLion has some sort of declarative macros support, while proc ones are in very early stages yet. So I wouldn't expect it to be around soon.
I apologise for being so defensive but having mismatching types for iter items is really a dealbreaker for me. :(

You need to have "proc_macro resolution" set up in rust analyzer, which isn't yet enabled by default iirc. No clue if CLion does that or not.

As an aside: does query resolution work for Bevy 0.4 using rust-analyzer or CLion?  In 0.5 we moved to proc macros for `all_tuples!` to improve docs + implementation clarity. Prior to that we were using `macro_rules!`.

Given that RA does have support for proc macros (and I'm _hoping_ CLion also already has support or its in the works), idk if its worth reverting the change at this point. But its worth discussing.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2694663/152664213-c85fb9a2-07d5-4c66-9be4-ca50a95eaadf.png)

Oh, weird, I had those flags enabled... I opened the project once more, and I indeed can see all the type hints in the VSCode now, even for the generated structs.
I also was able to get the type hints for CLion! Turned out, I had `org.rust.macros.proc` enabled, but I was missing the `org.rust.cargo.evaluate.build.scripts` flag, which was also required.

> Given that RA does have support for proc macros (and I'm hoping CLion also already has support or its in the works), idk if its worth reverting the change at this point. But its worth discussing.

That appears to be a false alert, sorry. :D

Alright, I guess I'm convinced to introduce the additional generated struct for mapping `&mut T` to `Mut<T>`. :)

@alice-i-cecile @cart I also wanted to ask your opinions on naming conventions for the structs.
Should custom queries have `Query` suffix? Currently, in my examples I use the following:
```rust
#[derive(WorldQuery)]
pub struct HealthQuery<'w> { ... }
```

Which generates the following structures:
```
HealthQueryState
HealthQueryFetch
HealthQueryReadOnly // this one isn't generated for filters
```

I guess with the introduction of another struct we can have the following names:
```
HealthQueryState
HealthQueryFetch
// The following two won't be generated for filters:
HealthQueryItem // this one will map `&mut T` to `Mut<T>`
HealthQueryReadOnlyItem
```

My very minor concern is the tautology in `Query<HealthQuery>`. Though the suffix seems to make sense for filters (for example, `HasHealthFilter`). So suggesting to suffix structs with either `Query` or `Filter` will be consistent from this kind of perspective.

> Should custom queries have Query suffix?

IMO yes.

> Should custom queries have Query suffix?

Yeah I think they should. Non-suffixed things we query for are "actual component data", whereas this is "sets of components". Seems reasonable to disambiguate. Lets default to "suffixes as a convention" for now and we can revisit later if use cases dictate otherwise.
@cart @alice-i-cecile I've just pushed a change dropping the `FetchedItem` trait and adding a new struct for returned query items.

Looks good to me! Now that this impl is a bit more straightforward, I think we can save on some code complexity / redundancy by consolidating under a single WorldQuery derive impl.

Just to illustrate (this has a number of issues in the impl, but I've gotta move on to other stuff), I started shuffling stuff around: https://gist.github.com/cart/0cc7d3ba293abdf5070bb529a41c9bf6

This refactor cuts down on hundreds of lines of code, which seems worthwhile.

Thanks for gist! I'll try to finish it. I've also noticed that you commented out the `dead_code` workaround, just wanted to clarify: did you comment it out cause it got broken or did you try to get rid of it completely?
I was planning on testing whether it was still necessary under the new impl. It feels like we shouldn't need it, given that we're using the same pattern as the built in Fetch impls.

@cart done. I was even able to get rid of the TODO that I had previously left for the `ReadOnly` impl.
The `dead_code` workaround is still needed though, as original struct's fields are never read by anything (the `Item` types are used by the user's code instead).
Looks good to me! Fantastic work!

issue_context.title: Component Bundle Queries
issue_context.body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

Reduce the verbosity of queries by using bundles, which are already used for this purpose during entity archetype construction.

## What solution would you like?

The ability to add a struct that derives `Bundle` to a query, and have it return with its fields accessible as components. E.g.:

```rust
#[derive(Bundle)]
struct Transform {
    translation: Translation,
    rotation: Rotation,
    scale: Scale,
}

// can still use this common case
Query<&Transform>

// but also, able to query fields granularly with change detection
Query<&Transform, Changed<Rotation>>
//...

// Can use this to group other sets of components as query-able bundles
#[derive(Bundle)]
struct Dog {
    legs: Legs
    fluffy_tail: Tail
    wet_nose: Nose
}
// These two queries are functionally equivalent, but the `Dog` query returns a list of `Dog` structs
Query<&Dog>
Query<(&Legs, &Tail, &Nose)>
```

## What alternative(s) have you considered?

Most of this can already be achieved with some verbosity, as shown in the dog example above. However, it would also allow us to split apart common components like `Transform` into their parts with _field level change detection_, without losing the ergonomics of the `Transform` type.

## Additional context

Similar to #786
comments:
It seems clear that when operating in this way, `With` and `Without` should use AND logic.

However for `Added / Changed / Removed` (see #2148), the intuitive behavior is actually different.

For `Added`, it should trigger if and only if the entity now satisfies the `With` criteria, and did not before. `Removed` is then the opposite.

For `Changed`, it should trigger if any of the components are changed, which is a both intuitive and a nice ergonomic win for `Or`-logic query filtering in the most common cases.

>To break down the desired behavior a bit, I think it should work like so when iterated over.
>
>```rust
>let query = Query<&Transform>
>
>for (translation, rotation, scale) in query.iter(){
>
>}
>```

I think I'd actually prefer it if the query returned the struct, though I'm not sure which is easier to implement. One reason to return the struct is because you can then implement methods for the bundle, it would also mean this isn't (as much of) a breaking change, because querying a `Transform` would still return a `Transform`.

Ah, there was a fourth case I forget to mention:
```rust
let query = Query<&Transform>

for transform in query.iter(){

}
```

As I'm trying to hint at by example, the idea is that the compiler either keeps the struct intact or automatically unpacks it based on the number of arguments it has to match against.
As part of this change, we could remove [`WithBundle`](https://docs.rs/bevy/0.5.0/bevy/ecs/prelude/struct.WithBundle.html), cleaning up our API in a more consistent way.

>  Currently the bundle filter will match anything that has all components in a bundle, but imo the filter would be more useful / aligned with user intent if it only matched things that actually added the Bundle.

- @cart in #2255 

I really dislike this behavior: it's incredibly magical, special-cases bundles and forces us to store Bundle identity on the entity. Instead, I would prefer to promote the use of "defining" marker components as the first item of each bundle.

This is a natural and useful pattern in end-user code, and you can get the effect you're looking for because no other entities should have that unique marker unless they include the bundle (especially if you don't export the marker's type).

The other benefit of that design is that it dovetails really nicely with the entity inspection patterns discussed in #1467, particularly for a visual editor, where you want to quickly learn the "types" of an entity (in which case you look at the "defining" components of the bundle).

I responded in #2255 [here](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/issues/2255#issuecomment-848380032), but I will reiterate my perspective here.

In short, my desired behavior for bundle queries is:

Match anything with all components in the bundle (a bundle filter), but return the result from the query as the bundle struct. This retains the current composability of entities, adds the ergonomics of allowing traits/methods over bundles, without the magic of bundles being semantically "special".

I also agree with @alice-i-cecile in that I don't like bundles being "special-cases" or "magical". I mostly don't like that it directly interferes with the composability that we get with only defining archetypes from components.

Obviously, you can't use the `Transform` name for destructing, as has been brought up every time this has been asked for before.

(Because Transform takes owned fields)

Also, I think this issue's discussion is conflating two or three things:
- Splitting Transform back into a bundle again (I don't trust the performance characteristics of this)
- (Per field change tracking, which could be useful but I think is likely to have more overhead than its worth)
- Bundle convenience queries (potentially useful, although I feel like it encourages bad patterns where you query for more components than you need to, which has some performance cost. As it happens, the unused 'found' component pointers won't be derefed, so it shouldn't be too bad)

Something I have not seen discussed, is that this would have been useful for **refactoring a component into multiple components**, since the original component struct could be changed to derive bundle. 

If, for example, you wanted to split `Velocity{ linear: Vec3, angular: Vec3 }` into LinVel and AngVel components. 

The concern for foot-gunning here I think is applicable to larger bundles. However, going in the opposite direction (as above) there could be opportunity to use bundles to make one's codebase *more modular* instead of less, and in cases where it would otherwise be non-ergonomic or a refactor burden to do so. This is especially relevant to rapid-prototyping.

This could be accomplished with a different derive + trait (seperate from bundle), however the existing WorldQuery machinery (as far as I can tell) cannot be made generic over mutability, and is not drop-in the way I'm describing.
